title: Chained Exchange Rates
statement:
A game has its own currencies. You get known exchange rates: pairs[i] = [a, b] with rates[i] = v means one unit of a is worth v units of b. Rates work in both directions, so one b is worth 1 / v of a, and rates multiply along a chain of exchanges.

For each query [c, d], return how many units of d one unit of c is worth. Return -1 if the answer cannot be worked out from the given rates: either currency never appears in pairs, or no chain connects them. A currency that does appear is worth exactly 1 of itself.

The given rates never contradict each other. Answers within 10⁻⁵ relative error are accepted.

examples.why: gold → silver → copper multiplies 10 × 20. Going backwards divides: 1 / 20. "iron" is never mentioned, so even iron-to-iron is unknown.
{a, b} and {c, d} are separate groups, so a to d has no chain. b is known, so b to b is 1.

constraints: Currency names are 1–5 lowercase letters or digits
0 < rates[i] ≤ 20, and the rates are consistent
hints: Draw each currency as a node and each rate as an edge. What does a chain of exchanges look like in that picture?
Store each rate as two directed edges: a → b with weight v and b → a with weight 1 / v. A query is then a path search that multiplies weights along the way.
For each query, run a DFS or BFS from c, carrying the product so far, and stop when you reach d. Check first that both names exist; that alone answers the c = c case.

explain.intuition:
An exchange rate is an edge between two currencies with a weight, and going against the edge uses the inverse weight. If gold → silver is 10 and silver → copper is 20, then gold → copper is the product along the path, 200. So every query is "find any path from c to d in this graph and multiply the weights on it".

Because the rates are consistent, any path gives the same product, so you can take the first one a DFS finds. If the search never reaches d, the two currencies are in different groups and the answer is unknown. A faster alternative for many queries is a weighted union-find that stores each currency's value relative to its group's root; then c to d is value(c) / value(d) when both share a root.
steps: Build an adjacency map: for each pair [a, b] with rate v, add a → b with weight v and b → a with weight 1 / v.
For a query [c, d], return -1 if either name is missing from the map.
Otherwise search from c with a stack of (node, product) and a visited set.
When you pop d, return its product. If the stack empties first, return -1.
pitfalls: Answering 1 for [x, x] when x never appears in the rates. Unknown stays unknown.
Adding only the forward edge. A query may need to walk an edge backwards, which uses 1 / v.
Forgetting the visited set. The graph can have cycles, and the search would loop forever.

complexity.time: O(q · (V + E)) with a search per query

solutions.title: Path search per query
solutions.idea: Turn rates into a weighted graph with inverse back edges, then DFS from c to d multiplying weights.

solutions.title: Weighted union-find
solutions.idea: Each currency stores its worth in units of its parent. Path compression keeps that worth relative to the root, and c to d is worth(c) / worth(d) when they share a root.

followups: The rates may now contradict each other. How would you detect an inconsistent set?
Rates keep arriving while queries are asked in between. Which of the two approaches handles that better?
